ledger.claim: A device is not fully owned when its maker can disable features after sale.
ledger.request_basis: a device is not fully owned when its maker can disable features after sale

sentences.text: The device is yours right up until the maker reaches through the network and switches off part of it.
That sounds like ownership only if we define ownership as the right to hold an object while somebody else retains the right to decide what it can do.
You paid for the thing, you carried it home, and you were told – explicitly or by implication – that the transaction had ended.
But the transaction hasn't ended if the seller can keep changing the bargain after you've paid.
Imagine buying a refrigerator whose coldness depended on an escrow agent.
The agent doesn't own the refrigerator, naturally; it merely holds the switch that makes the compressor run.
If you miss a payment, violate a rule, or simply fall outside the agent's preferred business model, the refrigerator becomes a very expensive cupboard (a cupboard with excellent branding, of course).
Would you say you owned the refrigerator?
You'd say you possessed it, perhaps, in the same way you possess a hotel room until checkout.
The distinction matters because possession is temporary control, while ownership is the authority to use the object without seeking permission from the party that sold it.
Digital features turn that distinction into a business model.
A maker can sell you a physical object and reserve a remote veto over the functions that made the object worth buying in the first place.

The device sits on your desk, in your pocket, or in your driveway, but the decisive part of it lives somewhere else – in an account, a server, a licence, or a policy written in language designed to be skimmed and forgotten.
You aren't merely buying a tool; you're buying a tool-shaped dependency.
And when the dependency is withdrawn, the maker will often describe the result as an adjustment, an update, or a safety measure.
That vocabulary is doing suspiciously heavy lifting.
Of course, a maker may have legitimate reasons to change software or disable a dangerous function.
I think the answer to that problem is a narrower power, clearly disclosed and bounded by rules you can understand – not a permanent claim over an object you've already bought.
Otherwise every promise attached to the device is provisional, and every feature is rented whether the receipt says so or not.
That isn't a technical footnote; it's the central condition of the sale.
The usual defence is that you agreed to the terms.
You clicked through them, they say, so what could be unfair about the consequences?
Quite a lot, actually.

Agreement doesn't magically turn a one-sided power into a fair exchange, especially when refusing the terms means refusing the product altogether (the classic choice between consent and walking away).
If the maker can disable features after sale, the question isn't whether you accepted words on a screen; it's whether those words cancel the ordinary meaning of purchase.
Calling that ownership is bullshit.
We should stop treating this as a quarrel over terminology.
Words matter because they assign power, and the word ownership has traditionally carried a limit on the seller's continuing control.
When we let a maker retain a kill switch, we let the seller remain present inside the sale forever.
You don't need to be a lawyer to see the problem; you only need to imagine the same arrangement in a shop selling chairs, lamps, or refrigerators.
The absurdity becomes visible when the cloud disappears.
That doesn't mean every device must be frozen in time the moment you buy it.
We can permit repairs, updates, replacements, and safety interventions while still insisting that the buyer's control is real.
The maker can offer a service, but it shouldn't disguise a service as ownership and then punish you when the service changes.
If the feature is essential to the product's ordinary use, disabling it should require a justification stronger than a revised revenue plan.
And if the maker wants a revocable licence, it should sell a revocable licence in plain language.
I keep coming back to the refrigerator because the object makes the power relationship impossible to ignore.
The compressor isn't yours if somebody else can turn it off, and the feature isn't yours if somebody else can revoke it.
We can argue about interfaces, servers, and software architecture until the batteries die.
The underlying question remains stubbornly simple: who gets the final say over the thing you bought?
If the answer is the maker, you bought possession with a landlord hiding inside it.
That is not full ownership.
